Curating an ML-Ready Dataset from Crowd-Sourced Hardware Records¶

A case study on California EV charging equipment (Open Charge Map) with EDA and TensorFlow¶

Question. Crowd-sourced hardware data is messy. How much of the work of getting a trustworthy model comes from dataset curation (validation, cleaning, versioning, leakage control, honest splits) versus model choice? We use California EV charging hardware records to predict the rated power (kW) of a charger connector, and we measure what a TensorFlow model adds over simple baselines.

Pipeline in this notebook

  1. Audit the raw data (missingness, label noise, geographic errors, leakage risks)
  2. Clean with explicit, logged rules (a cleaning ledger)
  3. Version the dataset (v1 raw, v2 clean, model-ready) with a manifest and checksums
  4. Exploratory data analysis
  5. Leakage-safe splits (grouped by charging location)
  6. Baselines (median, per-connector median, Ridge, gradient boosting) plus a feature ablation
  7. TensorFlow model with embeddings, multiple seeds, optional Weights & Biases tracking
  8. Error analysis, limitations, and data governance notes

Data. data/raw/california_ev_chargers.csv, produced by scripts/ocm_california.py from the ocm-export repository (Open Charge Map). One row = one group of identical connectors at a charging location. Licenses vary by data provider; see the governance section.

def sha256(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(1 << 20), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()

Audit findings that drive the design

  • Some records labelled California are physically elsewhere (e.g. Georgia, Wisconsin, Hawaii, China), so the state label alone is not a trustworthy filter.
  • charge_level is a bucketed version of the target, and amps x voltage reconstructs it. Using either would give a model that looks excellent and learns nothing. Both are excluded and treated as leakage.
  • A small number of rows have a level label that contradicts the kW value. These are suspect labels and are held out of the model-ready set rather than silently fixed.
  • connector_status and number_of_points are mostly missing, so they are not used.

2. Cleaning with a ledger¶

Every rule is explicit, and the number of rows each rule removes is recorded. The ledger is saved with the dataset so a reviewer can see exactly how v2 was derived from v1.

In [5]:
STR_COLS = ["name", "address", "city", "state", "operator", "usage_type", "connection_type", "current_type"]
df = raw.copy()
for c in STR_COLS:
    df[c] = df[c].astype("string").str.strip()
df["city"] = df["city"].str.title()

ledger = []
def step(rule, before, after, why):
    ledger.append({"rule": rule, "rows_before": len(before), "rows_after": len(after),
                   "removed": len(before) - len(after), "why": why})

d1 = df[df.latitude.between(*CA_LAT) & df.longitude.between(*CA_LON)]
step("R1 coordinates inside California", df, d1, "State label says CA but the coordinates are elsewhere")
d2 = d1.drop_duplicates()
step("R2 drop exact duplicate rows", d1, d2, "Identical records inflate counts and leak across splits")

v2 = d2.reset_index(drop=True).copy()
for c in ["operator", "usage_type", "current_type", "city", "connection_type"]:
    v2[c] = v2[c].fillna("Unknown")

lvl = v2.charge_level.astype("string")
is_l1 = lvl.str.startswith("Level 1").fillna(False).astype(bool)
is_l3 = lvl.str.startswith("Level 3").fillna(False).astype(bool)
v2["flag_missing_target"] = v2.power_kw.isna()
v2["flag_level_kw_mismatch"] = (is_l1 & (v2.power_kw >= 7)) | (is_l3 & (v2.power_kw < 20))

d3 = v2[~v2.flag_missing_target]
step("R3 require a power_kw value", v2, d3, "Cannot train or evaluate without the target")
d4 = d3[~d3.flag_level_kw_mismatch]
step("R4 drop level/kW contradictions", d3, d4, "Suspect labels: level bucket disagrees with the kW value")
model_ready = d4.reset_index(drop=True).copy()

ledger_df = pd.DataFrame(ledger)
ledger_df

3. Dataset versioning¶

Three versions are written with SHA-256 checksums and a manifest, which is the same idea as DVC or a W&B Artifact in a larger setup.

Version Contents
v1 Raw export, unmodified (checksum only)
v2 Cleaned, all rows retained, with quality flags
model-ready v2 minus rows without a usable target

5. Leakage-safe splits¶

A location often has several rows (for example, several connector groups at one site). A random row split would put near-identical rows in train and test, which inflates scores. We split by poi_id (70 / 15 / 15), and all category vocabularies and scalers are fitted on the training set only.

In [14]:
mr = model_ready.copy()
gss = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.30, random_state=SEED)
tr_i, tmp_i = next(gss.split(mr, groups=mr.poi_id))
tmp = mr.iloc[tmp_i]
gss2 = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.50, random_state=SEED)
va_rel, te_rel = next(gss2.split(tmp, groups=tmp.poi_id))
mr["split"] = ""
mr.loc[mr.index[tr_i], "split"] = "train"
mr.loc[tmp.index[va_rel], "split"] = "val"
mr.loc[tmp.index[te_rel], "split"] = "test"

ids = {s: set(mr.loc[mr.split == s, "poi_id"]) for s in ["train", "val", "test"]}
assert not (ids["train"] & ids["val"]) and not (ids["train"] & ids["test"]) and not (ids["val"] & ids["test"]), "location leakage!"
print("no charging location appears in more than one split")

summary = mr.groupby("split").agg(rows=("power_kw", "size"), locations=("poi_id", "nunique"),
                                   median_kw=("power_kw", "median"), dc_fast_share=("power_kw", lambda s: (s >= 40).mean()))
mr.to_parquet(PROC / "ev_ca_model_ready_with_splits.parquet", index=False)
summary.loc[["train", "val", "test"]]

6. Feature preparation and baselines¶

Target: log(power_kw), because the distribution is heavy-tailed. Metrics are reported back on the kW scale.

Features: connection_type, current_type, operator, usage_type, city, latitude, longitude, connector_quantity.

Baselines (simple to complex): global median, per-connector-type median, Ridge on one-hot features, and gradient boosting.

In [15]:
CAT = ["connection_type", "current_type", "operator", "usage_type", "city"]
NUM = ["latitude", "longitude", "log_quantity"]
MIN_COUNT = {"connection_type": 10, "current_type": 1, "operator": 20, "usage_type": 10, "city": 25}

mr["log_quantity"] = np.log1p(mr.connector_quantity.fillna(1).clip(0, 50))
mr["y"] = np.log(mr.power_kw.clip(lower=1))
train, val, test = (mr[mr.split == s].reset_index(drop=True) for s in ["train", "val", "test"])

vocabs = {}
for c in CAT:
    vc = train[c].value_counts()
    vocabs[c] = ["__other__"] + sorted(vc[vc >= MIN_COUNT[c]].index.tolist())
maps = {c: {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vocabs[c])} for c in CAT}
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(train[NUM])

def featurize(frame):
    out = pd.DataFrame({c: frame[c].astype(object).map(maps[c]).fillna(0).astype(int) for c in CAT})
    out[NUM] = scaler.transform(frame[NUM])
    return out

F = {"train": featurize(train), "val": featurize(val), "test": featurize(test)}
Y = {"train": train.y.to_numpy(), "val": val.y.to_numpy(), "test": test.y.to_numpy()}
KW = {"train": train.power_kw.to_numpy(), "val": val.power_kw.to_numpy(), "test": test.power_kw.to_numpy()}
print({c: len(v) for c, v in vocabs.items()}, "<- vocabulary sizes (incl. __other__)")
print({k: v.shape for k, v in F.items()})

def kw_metrics(y_log_pred, split):
    pred = np.clip(np.exp(y_log_pred), 1, 400)
    true = KW[split]
    return {
        "MAE_kW": mean_absolute_error(true, pred),
        "MedAE_kW": median_absolute_error(true, pred),
        "RMSE_kW": float(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(true, pred))),
        "R2_kW": r2_score(true, pred),
        "MAE_log": mean_absolute_error(Y[split], y_log_pred),
    }

results = {}   # name -> {"val": metrics, "test": metrics}
preds = {}     # name -> {"val": log-pred, "test": log-pred}
def record(name, p_val, p_test):
    results[name] = {"val": kw_metrics(p_val, "val"), "test": kw_metrics(p_test, "test")}
    preds[name] = {"val": p_val, "test": p_test}
    log_local({"model": name, "val": results[name]["val"], "test": results[name]["test"]})

# 1) global median
g = np.median(Y["train"])
record("Global median", np.full(len(Y["val"]), g), np.full(len(Y["test"]), g))

# 2) per-connector-type median (a one-feature lookup table)
med = train.groupby("connection_type").y.median()
def conn_median(frame):
    return frame.connection_type.map(med).fillna(g).to_numpy()
record("Connector-type median", conn_median(val), conn_median(test))

# 3) Ridge on one-hot features
ridge = make_pipeline(
    ColumnTransformer([("oh", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), CAT)], remainder="passthrough"),
    Ridge(alpha=1.0))
ridge.fit(F["train"], Y["train"])
record("Ridge (one-hot)", ridge.predict(F["val"]), ridge.predict(F["test"]))

# 4) gradient boosting with native categorical support
def make_hgb(cols):
    return HistGradientBoostingRegressor(
        categorical_features=[c in CAT for c in cols], max_iter=250, learning_rate=0.08,
        max_leaf_nodes=31, l2_regularization=1.0, early_stopping=False, random_state=SEED)
ALL = CAT + NUM
hgb = make_hgb(ALL).fit(F["train"][ALL], Y["train"])
record("Gradient boosting", hgb.predict(F["val"][ALL]), hgb.predict(F["test"][ALL]))

7. TensorFlow model¶

A multi-input Keras network: each categorical feature has its own embedding, which is concatenated with the standardised numeric features and passed through a small MLP. Loss is Huber on the log target (robust to the heavy tail). Three seeds are trained, which gives a spread and a seed ensemble.

In [18]:
def emb_dim(n):
    return int(min(8, max(2, np.ceil(n / 2))))

def build_model(seed):
    tf.keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    inputs, embs = {}, []
    for c in CAT:
        inp = tf.keras.Input(shape=(1,), name=c, dtype="int32")
        inputs[c] = inp
        e = tf.keras.layers.Embedding(len(vocabs[c]), emb_dim(len(vocabs[c])), name=f"emb_{c}")(inp)
        embs.append(tf.keras.layers.Flatten()(e))
    num = tf.keras.Input(shape=(len(NUM),), name="numeric")
    inputs["numeric"] = num
    x = tf.keras.layers.Concatenate()(embs + [num])
    x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")(x)
    x = tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.1)(x)
    x = tf.keras.layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(x)
    out = tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, name="log_power")(x)
    model = tf.keras.Model(inputs, out)
    model.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), loss=tf.keras.losses.Huber(delta=0.5),
                  metrics=[tf.keras.metrics.MeanAbsoluteError(name="mae")])
    return model

def tf_inputs(split):
    d = {c: F[split][c].to_numpy().reshape(-1, 1).astype("int32") for c in CAT}
    d["numeric"] = F[split][NUM].to_numpy().astype("float32")
    return d

build_model(0).summary()

histories, tf_val, tf_test, models_ = {}, [], [], {}
for seed in CONFIG["seeds"]:
    model = build_model(seed)
    cb = [tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=CONFIG["patience"], restore_best_weights=True),
          tf.keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=5, min_lr=1e-5)]
    h = model.fit(tf_inputs("train"), Y["train"], validation_data=(tf_inputs("val"), Y["val"]),
                  epochs=CONFIG["max_epochs"], batch_size=CONFIG["batch_size"], callbacks=cb, verbose=0)
    histories[seed] = h.history
    models_[seed] = model
    pv = model.predict(tf_inputs("val"), verbose=0).ravel()
    pt = model.predict(tf_inputs("test"), verbose=0).ravel()
    tf_val.append(pv); tf_test.append(pt)
    record(f"TensorFlow (seed {seed})", pv, pt)
    print(f"seed {seed}: {len(h.history['loss'])} epochs | val MAE {results[f'TensorFlow (seed {seed})']['val']['MAE_kW']:.2f} kW")
    if run:
        for ep in range(len(h.history["loss"])):
            run.log({f"seed{seed}/{k}": v[ep] for k, v in h.history.items()})

Key findings¶

1. Curation mattered before any model was trained. Of 21,952 raw rows, 2.3% were removed: 15 records labelled California but located in other states or countries, 107 exact duplicates, 373 with no power value, and 4 with a level label that contradicted the kW value. Two features (charge_level and amps/voltage) were excluded because they encode the target, and splits were grouped by charging location (no location appears in more than one split).

2. Most of the accuracy comes from simple structure, not model complexity. Test MAE (kW, lower is better):

Model MAE (kW) R²
Global median 27.2 -0.15
Connector-type median 15.8 0.30
Ridge (one-hot) 12.7 0.67
Gradient boosting 9.6 0.76
TensorFlow (seed 0 / 3-seed ensemble) 9.6 / 9.7 0.75 / 0.75

Across three seeds, TensorFlow scores 9.78 ± 0.18 kW MAE. It matches gradient boosting but does not beat it. This is a common outcome on small tabular data (about 15,000 training rows), and it is worth reporting honestly. The practical gain came from moving off the baselines (27.2 to 9.6 kW), not from choosing a neural network over trees.

3. Operator is the most informative feature after connector type (validation ablation). Removing operator raises MAE from 9.6 to 12.2 kW; connector type alone gives 16.5 kW; location alone has no predictive skill (R² of -0.07). Removing location features actually lowered validation MAE slightly (9.58 to 9.17 kW), which suggests latitude, longitude and city add noise rather than signal for this target.

4. Errors concentrate in high-power DC fast chargers. The median absolute error is only about 0.13 kW, because most connectors are standard Level 2 ratings. The mean and RMSE are dominated by the tail: MAE is 0.21 kW for connectors under 7.4 kW but about 110 kW for 100-400 kW connectors. NACS (66 kW MAE) and CCS (43 kW MAE) are hardest, because the same connector type is installed at many different power ratings (for example 50, 150, 250 and 350 kW), and the available features cannot tell them apart.

What this suggests¶

Better data curation and feature choice moved the error far more than architecture did. The most promising next steps are features that describe the site (for example, the mix of connectors at a location, or network-specific hardware generations), and a TensorFlow variant without location features, chosen on the validation set. Neither is claimed here, since the test set was used only once.

9. Limitations¶

  • No usage or reliability data. The dataset describes hardware and location only, so this study predicts a specification, not demand or failures.
  • Crowd-sourced labels. Records may be stale or wrong, which is why the validation layer exists. Last-verified dates reach back years.
  • Not a causal claim. Location features capture where networks deploy certain hardware, not why.
  • date_created is not an install date. It spikes in specific years because of bulk imports, so no time-trend analysis is attempted.
  • One state, one snapshot. Results may not transfer to other regions or later data.

10. Data governance notes¶

  • Provenance: every version has a SHA-256 checksum, and every dropped row is accounted for in the cleaning ledger (data/processed/manifest.json).
  • Licensing: Open Charge Map attributes a data provider and license to each record. Records from contributors use the Open Charge Map license; others vary. Attribution is required, and the provider licenses should be reviewed before any redistribution of derived data.
  • Sensitivity: the data contains business locations and operator names. It contains no personal data. Contact fields in the source (for example phone numbers) were deliberately not carried into this dataset.
  • Leakage controls: target-derived columns are excluded, splits are grouped by location, and vocabularies and scalers are fit on the training set only.
  • Reproducibility: fixed seeds, pinned requirements, and the environment is recorded below.
